key_findings.finding: Yes. In the primary study “TRAIL receptor deletion in mice suppresses the inflammation of nutrient excess” (PMID 25445398; J Hepatol 2015), mice with genetic deletion of the single murine TRAIL receptor (commonly called TRAIL-R/DR5; the mouse ortholog corresponding to human TNFRSF10B/DR5, with mice lacking separate TNFRSF10A/TNFRSF10B receptor paralogs) were fed a high-saturated-fat/high-cholesterol/high-fructose (FFC) diet. Compared with wild-type littermates, receptor-null mice had strongly reduced weight gain/adiposity and insulin resistance, suppressed steatohepatitis, near-normal ALT, less hepatocyte apoptosis and hepatic triglyceride accumulation, and diminished accumulation/activation of inflammatory macrophages in liver and adipose tissue. Bone-marrow macrophages from receptor-null mice also showed reduced chemotaxis and NF-κB activation in response to palmitate or LPS. The authors concluded that macrophage-associated hepatic and adipose inflammation from nutrient excess requires TRAIL-receptor signaling.

source_tools.relevance: Direct primary-study abstract and results preview with model, receptor deletion, and inflammatory/metabolic outcomes

key_findings.finding: The receptor-deletion result is distinct from TRAIL-ligand deletion. In a separate primary study (PMID 29124251; Hepatology Communications 2017), Trail−/− mice on the same type of FFC diet had reduced hepatic steatosis, ALT, hepatocyte death, macrophage-associated liver inflammation, stellate-cell activation, and collagen deposition, but no improvement in adipose-tissue injury/inflammation and aggravated insulin resistance. The paper explicitly states that mice have one TRAIL-receptor ortholog corresponding to the closely related human TRAIL-R1/TNFRSF10A and TRAIL-R2/TNFRSF10B system and refers to it as TRAIL-R/DR5. Thus, ligand knockout supports a liver-protective effect but does not reproduce the receptor-null adipose anti-inflammatory phenotype.

source_tools.relevance: Direct primary-study abstract and full-text preview distinguishing ligand knockout from receptor knockout and identifying the murine receptor nomenclature

key_findings.finding: Overall conclusion: deletion/knockout of the murine TRAIL receptor suppresses nutrient-excess-associated inflammation in the reported FFC-diet model, especially inflammatory macrophage accumulation/activation in liver and adipose tissue, whereas the evidence base identified here is for the single murine receptor (TRAIL-R/DR5, generally mapped to Tnfrsf10b), not independent mouse knockouts of both human-equivalent TNFRSF10A and TNFRSF10B.

source_tools.relevance: Primary paper documenting one murine TRAIL receptor ortholog and contrasting Trail−/− effects
